reason: Pollen sac size is given as a length in mm.
Stipules can be dilated or expanded at the base. The examples are correct.
Hyaline awns or awn parts are thin and transparent. Hyaline maps to transparent.
Perigynium teeth, face or tip can be hyaline. Some examples name a part of the perigynium (teeth, tip), not the whole.
A leaf sheath can be thickened. The 'hyaline margins' example is about the margins, not the sheath.
A lamina apex can be notched. The statement is about the apex, but the lamina is acceptable.
Capsule orientation (ascending, spreading, pendent) is a normal character.
Branches can bear bristly hairs, so bristly is a valid indumentum.

The examples (apex deflected downward, apical half geniculate) look like they describe other parts, not a corolla lip. A rule would need the bearer of the 'bent' phrase to be a corolla lip. It is not enough that the lip is the nearest part.
Cone shapes such as ovoid, globose and cylindric are convex 3-D shapes. The specific shape would be better, but the pair is valid.
Wrong reading: 'auricles 1-7.5 mm' is a length, not a count. A count of auricles would be 'amount' only for statements like '2 auricles'.
A flexuous peduncle is a wavy or sinuous one, which fits.
The ochrea surface can be papillose or scabrid, so texture applies. Some examples concern leaf blades, not the ochrea.
Capsule bases and necks can taper. The 'neck' examples describe a part of the capsule.
Cells, as in bryophyte leaf cells, can be coloured (brownish, greenish).
Teeth have a width, given in 'length × width' dimensions.

'Discs 10-30 × 12-20 mm' is probably the disc of an Asteraceae head, not the floral disc around the ovary. A rule would need family or context to tell the two apart. Statements like 'ca. 1 mm wide' fit a floral disc.

Most examples describe how deep the calyx is lobed ('parted to 1/3', 'lobed to 1/2'), which is a ratio of lobe to tube length. Only a few give a true depth in mm. A rule would need to route cleft fractions to a ratio or lobe-length quality.
Achenes can be minute or small, which maps to decreased size.
The adaxial epidermis of a sepal can be tomentose. The statements say 'adaxially tomentose'.
Leaf sheaths overlap, as in grasses and sedges.
An orchid labellum can be oblong.
Spore surface ornamentation (reticulate) is a spatial pattern. A specific reticulate value would be more precise.
Wrong part: 'Disk florets 14-25' counts the disc florets of a head, not floral discs. A floral disc is a single structure.
The perispore can be folded. Statements such as 'without folds' have to be read as absence.
A utricle can be truncate. Some examples describe the orifice or base, not the whole fruit.
An anther connective can be wide or widened.
The length-to-width ratio of anthers is a normal character. Some examples are about anther appendages.
A cyathium can be sessile or stalked.
A calyx can be annular or rim-like, as in a truncate calyx.
Drupes can be subglobose or subspherical.
The endostome can be present or absent. Statements such as 'endostome absent' need the negation read as absent.
Keel size is given as a height ('de haut').
Differentiation of moss leaves (perichaetial vs vegetative) is meaningful. Some examples are about laminal cells, not the leaf. A rule would need the bearer to be the leaf.
Chartaceous (papery) involucral bracts fit papyraceous.
Teeth can be spinose or spine-tipped. The pair is acceptable.
'Bladed' bracts have a blade, an expanded part. That is not 'blade-like' (resembling a blade). A rule would need to map 'bladed' to a different term, such as having a blade.
A perigynium base or body can be spongy, as in sedges.
A perigynium can be oblong.
A sepal base or apex can be cuneate. Some examples describe the sinus, not the sepal.
Branching can be sparse, and branches can bear sparse hairs. The sparse-hairs examples may belong to the hairs, not the branch.
An indusium can be thin.
Sepals or their margins can be translucent.
A viscidium can be elliptic.
Peristome teeth have a width.
Buds can be covered with silky (sericeous) hairs.
Internodes can be terete (round in section).
The number of internodes of an inflorescence axis is a count, so amount applies.
Pedicels can bear bristles. Some examples mention prickles, which are a different structure.
A leaflet lamina has colour, often given per surface (adaxial, abaxial).
Stems can be perennial. Some examples say 'basal perennial parts of stems'.
A leaf base can be truncate.
Pedicel orientation (suberect) is a normal character.
A leaflet margin can be entire.
Stipels can be present or absent. Negated statements need to be read as absent.
Stamens, mainly the filament, can be broadened. The pair is acceptable.
Pedicels can be hispidulous (minutely rough-haired).
Pollinia can be clavate.
The distance between pseudobulbs along a rhizome is a real character. The distance is between pseudobulbs, so it fits the bearer.
Bracteoles can be persistent or caducous.
